newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-U.S. defence firms chase Australian AEW order.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-U.S. defence firms chase Australian AEW order.

text.p: U.S. defence contractors are chasing the prize of an Australian launch order that analysts expect to determine which of them dominates a new sector of the aerospace market, mid-range airborne early warning systems.

Government sources in Canberra say the Australians cannot afford the top-line airborne warning and control systems (AWACS) aircraft that the Boeing Co has supplied to the U.S., Western Europe and Japan.
But the cheaper and less capable aircraft which are also available could never adequately patrol the vast and empty north-west of the Australian continent, they told Reuters.
"We need a mid-range system and we expect to be the first of several countries to operate one," said one defence source. "And we expect that our order may influence later buyers."

Defence analysts say the market cannot support all of the U.S. makers that hope to supply such aircraft -- Boeing, Lockheed Martin Corp, Northrop Grumman Corp and Raytheon Co, all of which were shortlisted by Canberra on Monday.
"The market is not big enough to support more than one, or at most two, mid-range systems," the editor of Australian Aviation magazine, Gerard Frawley, told Reuters.
The Australian contract is expected to be worth roughly $500 million for an initial order of at least four aircraft with more aircraft likely to follow.
As the first mid-range AEW contract, it will get one of the bidders into production and perhaps sway other countries looking for such equipment.

Boeing's airborne warning and control system (AWACS) is used by the United States, Britain, France and, co-operatively, the other Nato countries. Japan has also ordered AWACS, which is now mounted in Boeing's model 767 commercial airframe.
But that market is largely exhausted.
"No-one else can afford AWACS," said Frawley.

Defence sources in Canberra expect Boeing to offer its 737 commercial airframe for the Australian contract. The radar would be the fixed MESA radar, part of the Westinghouse defence-electronics business that Northrop Grumman bought this year.
One defence official said the 737 airframe would be cheap to maintain, since the model is commonly used by Australian domestic airlines,
But Northrop Grumman, in a joint venture with Lockheed Martin, is competing against Boeing with a different offer.
Northrop Grumman's E-2 Hawkeye radar plane, built for U.S. Navy aircraft carriers, does not have enough range for Australia.
So the joint venture is expected to propose the Hawkeye's APS-145 radar mounted in Lockheed's C-130J Hercules military transport airframe.
Again, the Hercules would offer no maintenance problem since the Royal Australian Air Force has operated it for more than 30 years and recently ordered a batch of the latest C-130J model.
Raytheon's E-Systems unit does not build aircraft at all but is expected to offer a radar system mounted in either a Boeing 737 or in an Airbus Industrie model, either the A320 or perhaps the A310.

A defence spokesman said the four companies had been shortlisted because they were judged capable of supplying the aircraft and of meeting requirements for security and Australian industry participation.
Defence Minister Ian MacLachlan said in a statement they would be invited later this year to respond to a request for proposals.
